item.title: “Monks, whatever a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon, that becomes the inclination of his mind. Monks, if a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon…
item.description:
“Monks, whatever a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon, that becomes the inclination of his mind. Monks, if a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon sensual thoughts, he has abandoned thoughts of renunciation. When his mind has become heavy with sensual thoughts, his mind inclines to sensual thoughts. Monks, if a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of ill-will … thoughts of harmfulness, he has abandoned thoughts of non-harmfulness. When his mind has become heavy with harmful thoughts, his mind inclines to harmful thoughts.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 19 – Dvedhāvitakkasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Form, monks, is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of form — that too is impermanent. Form that has arisen from the impermanent,…
item.description:
“Form, monks, is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of form — that too is impermanent. Form that has arisen from the impermanent, monks, how could it be permanent? Feeling, monks, is impermanent … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of consciousness — that too is impermanent. Consciousness that has arisen from the impermanent, monks, how could it be permanent? Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … disenchanted with feeling … disenchanted with perception … disenchanted with formations … disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate … He knows: ‘… there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.18
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the purification of beings?” “Mahāli, if form were exclusively happiness, immersed in happiness, accompanied…
item.description:
“What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the purification of beings?” “Mahāli, if form were exclusively happiness, immersed in happiness, accompanied by happiness, not accompanied by suffering, beings would not become disenchanted with form. But because form is suffering, Mahāli, immersed in suffering, accompanied by suffering, not accompanied by happiness, beings become disenchanted with form. Through disenchantment, they become dispassionate; through dispassion, they are liberated. This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the purification of beings. Such being the cause, such being the condition, beings are purified. If feeling … perception … formations … if consciousness were exclusively happiness … beings would not become disenchanted with consciousness. But because consciousness is suffering … beings become disenchanted with consciousness … and are liberated. This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the purification of beings.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.60
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Furthermore, Cunda, here a person is infatuated, addicted, living surrounded by the five strands of sensual pleasure; that is the fourth kind of pleasure. Cunda,…
item.description:
“Furthermore, Cunda, here a person is infatuated, addicted, living surrounded by the five strands of sensual pleasure; that is the fourth kind of pleasure. Cunda, these four kinds of pleasure are low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, unbeneficial, not leading to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna. Cunda, this is possible: wanderers of other sects might say: ‘The Sakyan ascetics are living addicted to these four kinds of pleasure.’ They should be answered: ‘That is not so; you speak wrongly. You misrepresent us, untruthfully, falsely.’”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 29 – Pāsādikasutta

item.title: "When the eye sees a form, the monk does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the…
item.description:
"When the eye sees a form, the monk does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — that cause the monk restrains, guards the eye faculty... By means of this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences an internal feeling of ease, unblemished."

From: Dīgha Nikāya 2 – Sāmaññaphalasutta

item.title: “Just as, monks, this body subsists in dependence on food, with food as condition it stands; without food it does not stand. So too, monks,…
item.description:
“Just as, monks, this body subsists in dependence on food, with food as condition it stands; without food it does not stand. So too, monks, the five hindrances subsist in dependence on food, with food as condition they stand; without food they do not stand. And what, monks, is the food for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire? There is, monks, the sign of the beautiful. Frequent unwise attention to it — this is the food for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.2
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, not knowing and not seeing the eye as it actually is; not knowing and not seeing forms … eye-consciousness … eye-contact as it actually…
item.description:
“Monks, not knowing and not seeing the eye as it actually is; not knowing and not seeing forms … eye-consciousness … eye-contact as it actually is; not knowing and not seeing the feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises dependent on eye-contact as it actually is, then he becomes attached to the eye, to forms, to eye-consciousness, to eye-contact. Dependent on eye-contact, the feeling—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises; he becomes attached to that feeling. When he dwells contemplating gratification, attached, tied, infatuated, the five aggregates of clinging accumulate for the future. And his craving—which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there—increases. His bodily torments increase, his mental torments increase, his bodily fevers increase, his mental fevers increase, his bodily pains increase, his mental pains increase. He experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 149 – Mahāsaḷāyatanikasutta

item.title: Then the Blessed One, knowing “This is Māra the Evil One,” recited this verse to Māra: Forms, sounds, tastes, and smells, And all contacts, all…
item.description:
Then the Blessed One, knowing “This is Māra the Evil One,” recited this verse to Māra:
Forms, sounds, tastes, and smells,
And all contacts, all phenomena —
These are terrifying things,
Bewildering beings in the world.
A disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One,
Mindful, transcends them all,
Transcending Māra’s power,
Shining like the sun.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.17
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, these five perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, ending in the deathless. What five? The…
item.description:
“Monks, these five perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, ending in the deathless. What five? The perception of impermanence, the perception of not-self, the perception of death, the perception of disgust with food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world. These five perceptions, monks, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, ending in the deathless.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.62

item.title: “Monks, a monk who thinks: ‘Covetousness, unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons the covetousness, unrighteous greed that is a…
item.description:
“Monks, a monk who thinks: ‘Covetousness, unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons the covetousness, unrighteous greed that is a defilement of the mind; thinks: ‘Ill-will is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons ill-will, the defilement of the mind; anger … hostility … hypocrisy … spite … envy … stinginess … deceit … fraud … obstinacy … impetuosity … conceit … arrogance … vanity; thinks: ‘Heedlessness is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons heedlessness, the defilement of the mind.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 7 – Vatthūpamasutta
